conventions.name: Cartesian Reference Frame
conventions.rule: Displacements along the surface are chosen positive in the direction of motion; upward perpendicular is positive normal.

conventions.name: Sign and Invariant Energy Conventions
conventions.rule: Potential energy is referenced to zero at the lowest point of interest ($U(0) = 0$). Work done by dissipative forces is zero in frictionless models.

units.unit_title: Mechanical Energy Conservation on a Frictionless Incline

demand_scaffolding.x: Conservation of mechanical energy on an inclined plane
demand_scaffolding.y: 1D work-energy theorem, vector resolution of gravity, and normal force orthogonality
demand_scaffolding.z: Decoupling ramp distance $s$ into vertical drop $h = s \sin\theta$ where non-conservative work $W_{\text{nc}} = 0$
demand_scaffolding.w: Observable exit task: derive the limiting case as $\theta \to 90^\circ$ and verify $v = \sqrt{2gh}$

entry_assumptions: Can apply the one-dimensional work-energy theorem $\Delta K = W_{\text{net}}$.
Can resolve force vectors into orthogonal Cartesian components.
Understands that work is the scalar product of force and displacement ($W = \vec{F} \cdot \Delta \vec{s}$).
units.inferential_jump: Proving that normal contact force does strictly zero work, so that mechanical energy depends solely on vertical altitude change $h = s \sin\theta$ independent of path length or mass.

steps.action: Analyze the work done by the normal contact force $\vec{N}$.
steps.why_valid: The normal force is perpendicular to the surface of the incline at all points, so $\vec{N} \cdot \Delta \vec{s} = N \Delta s \cos(90^\circ) = 0$.

steps.action: Resolve the gravitational force along the incline and compute work over distance $s$.
steps.why_valid: Component of gravity along the incline is $F_{\parallel} = mg \sin\theta$. Work done is $W_g = (mg \sin\theta)s = mg(s \sin\theta) = mgh$.

steps.action: Equate network done to change in kinetic energy ($u = 0$).
steps.why_valid: By the Work-Energy Theorem, $\Delta K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 - 0 = W_{\text{net}} = mgh$. Mass cancels from both sides.

units.equation_conditions: Valid for smooth surfaces where frictional dissipation is negligible ($\mu = 0$) under uniform gravity $g$.
units.worked_problem_stem: A 2.0 kg block is released from rest at the top of a smooth 30° incline of length 10 m. Calculate its speed at the base ($g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$).
worked_steps: Identify the given parameters: $m = 2.0\text{ kg}, s = 10\text{ m}, \theta = 30^\circ, g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$.
units.worked_conclusion: The block reaches the bottom with speed $v = \sqrt{98} \approx 9.90\text{ m/s}$, entirely independent of its 2.0 kg mass.
units.svg_caption: Mechanical Incline Progression: Force Decomposition $\to$ Height Projection $\to$ Velocity Derivation.
units.svg_body: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 200" width="100%" height="auto"><g data-g9-stage-id="s1"><polygon points="40,170 380,170 380,50" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="200" y="80" width="36" height="26" rx="4" fill="#bfdbfe" stroke="#1d4ed8" stroke-width="1.5" transform="rotate(21.8 200 80)"/><text x="80" y="160" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#2563eb">θ</text><text x="160" y="75" font-size="13" fill="#1e40af">s (ramp length)</text></g><g data-g9-stage-id="s2"><line x1="395" y1="50" x2="395" y2="170" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="4,4"/><text x="405" y="115" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">h = s sin θ</text><text x="210" y="50" font-size="13" fill="#16a34a">W_N = 0 (N ⊥ ds)</text></g><g data-g9-stage-id="s3"><rect x="40" y="15" width="380" height="30" rx="6" fill="#dcfce7" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="35" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#15803d">ΔK = mgh ⟹ v = √(2g s sin θ)</text></g></svg>
units.trap_wrong_idea: Assuming that the longer the incline, the more energy is lost or the slower the block travels, or multiplying gravity by $s$ directly ($mgs$) without the $\sin\theta$ factor.
units.trap_diagnostic: If an incline has length 20 m but the same vertical height $h = 5\text{ m}$, does the block reach the bottom with a different speed?
units.trap_repair_explanation: No. In the absence of friction, $v = \sqrt{2gh}$ depends purely on the vertical altitude drop $h$, not on the slope length $s$. The longer incline simply reduces acceleration while increasing travel time, yielding the exact same final speed.
units.triad_check: Why does the normal contact force do zero mechanical work on a sliding object?
units.triad_apply: A frictionless ramp has height $h = 20\text{ m}$. What is the speed of an object sliding from rest at the bottom ($g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$)?
units.triad_connect: How does this energy conservation principle extend to curved ramps and roller-coasters where the angle $\theta$ changes continuously?

exit_task.prompt: Evaluate the limiting behavior of the derived speed formula $v = \sqrt{2gs \sin\theta}$ as the angle $\theta \to 90^\circ$. What physical scenario does this represent, and does it agree with 1D vertical kinematics?
exit_task.answer: When $\theta \to 90^\circ$, $\sin(90^\circ) = 1$ and the incline length $s$ equals the vertical height $h$. The formula becomes $v = \sqrt{2gh}$, which identically reproduces the 1D free-fall velocity from rest.
exit_task.check: Independent 1D kinematic check: $v^2 = u^2 + 2g(\Delta y)$ with $u = 0$ gives $v = \sqrt{2gh}$. The limiting case matches 1D physics identically.

units.unit_title: Dimensional Synthesis of the Newton from Fundamental SI Base Units

demand_scaffolding.x: Derived unit Newton (N) in terms of fundamental dimensions
demand_scaffolding.y: Base SI units of mass (kg), length (m), and time (s)
demand_scaffolding.z: Dynamic definition from Newton's second law: $1\text{ N} \equiv 1\text{ kg} \cdot 1\text{ m/s}^2$
demand_scaffolding.w: Observable exit task: derive the base unit expression of momentum $p = mv$ and show $[F \times t] = [p]$

entry_assumptions: Familiarity with the 7 fundamental SI base quantities (specifically mass, length, time).
Understanding Newton's second law in algebraic form: $F = ma$.
units.inferential_jump: Understanding that derived SI units are not arbitrary names, but are structurally bound definitions dictated by governing physical laws.

steps.action: Identify the base SI quantities that form Newton's second law.
steps.why_valid: Mass is measured in kilograms ($\text{kg}$), and acceleration is change in velocity per unit time ($\text{m/s}^2$).

steps.action: Multiply base dimensions according to the product relation $F = ma$.
Bind the derived unit name (Newton) to this composite base product.
steps.why_valid: By international convention, 1 Newton is defined as the force giving 1 kg mass an acceleration of $1\text{ m/s}^2$.

units.equation_conditions: Universal definition in the International System of Units (SI).
units.worked_problem_stem: Express a force of $25\text{ N}$ acting on a $5.0\text{ kg}$ body in fundamental base units and compute the resulting acceleration.
worked_steps: Express force in base units: $25\text{ N} = 25\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}/\text{s}^2$.
units.worked_conclusion: The resulting acceleration is $5.0\text{ m/s}^2$, demonstrating dimensional cancellation.
units.svg_caption: Dimensional Synthesis: Base Quantities $\to$ Product Formulation $\to$ Derived Unit Binding.
units.svg_body: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 140" width="100%" height="auto"><g data-g9-stage-id="s1"><rect x="20" y="20" width="180" height="40" rx="6" fill="#e0e7ff" stroke="#4338ca"/><text x="110" y="45" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#312e81">Mass: kg</text><rect x="240" y="20" width="180" height="40" rx="6" fill="#e0e7ff" stroke="#4338ca"/><text x="330" y="45" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#312e81">Acceleration: m/s²</text></g><g data-g9-stage-id="s2"><line x1="220" y1="65" x2="220" y2="85" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2"/><text x="235" y="78" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#2563eb">F = m · a</text></g><g data-g9-stage-id="s3"><rect x="60" y="90" width="320" height="40" rx="8" fill="#fdf2f8" stroke="#db2777" stroke-width="2"/><text x="220" y="115" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#9d174d">1 Newton (N) = 1 kg·m/s²</text></g></svg>
units.trap_wrong_idea: Confusing force with energy (writing $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}^2$) or dividing by time instead of time squared.
units.trap_diagnostic: What is the difference between the base unit of force ($	ext{N}$) and the base unit of energy ($	ext{J}$)?
units.trap_repair_explanation: Energy is work ($F \times d$), which multiplies force by an extra meter: $1\text{ J} = 1\text{ N}\cdot\text{m} = 1\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}^2$. Force has length to power 1, whereas energy has length to power 2.
units.triad_check: What are the three fundamental SI base units that compose one Newton?
units.triad_apply: If an object has mass $0.5\text{ kg}$ and acceleration $4\text{ m/s}^2$, what net force in Newtons acts on it?
units.triad_connect: How is impulse defined as $J = F \Delta t$, and what are its base SI units?

exit_task.prompt: Determine the SI base unit composition of linear momentum $p = mv$. Then, prove that impulse $F \Delta t$ has identical SI base units.
exit_task.answer: Momentum $p = mv$ has base units $\text{kg} \times \text{m/s} = \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}/\text{s}$. Impulse is force $\times$ time: $[F \Delta t] = (\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}/\text{s}^2) \times \text{s} = \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}/\text{s}$. The base units are identical.
exit_task.check: Impulse-Momentum Theorem check: $\Delta p = F \Delta t$. Both sides share dimensional formula $[M][L][T]^{-1}$. Verified.

units.unit_title: The Factor Theorem and Remainder Vanishing from First Principles

demand_scaffolding.y: Division Algorithm for polynomials: $p(x) = (x - a)q(x) + r$
demand_scaffolding.z: Annihilation of quotient via $x = a$, giving remainder $r = p(a)$
demand_scaffolding.w: Verifying factor status of $(x - a)$ by evaluating $p(a)$

entry_assumptions: Polynomial Division Algorithm: Dividend = Divisor $\times$ Quotient + Remainder.
Remainder degree property: $\deg(r) < \deg(\text{divisor})$. For a linear divisor, $\deg(r) < 1 \implies r$ is a constant.
units.inferential_jump: Connecting polynomial remainder evaluation $p(a) = 0$ directly to exact algebraic divisibility $(x - a) \mid p(x)$.

steps.action: Set up the polynomial division equation for $p(x)$ divided by linear factor $(x - a)$.
steps.why_valid: Polynomial division algorithm guarantees unique quotient $q(x)$ and constant remainder $r$.
Setting $x = a$ annihilates the divisor: $(a - a)q(a) = 0 \cdot q(a) = 0$, leaving $p(a) = r$.
$(x - a)$ is a factor of $p(x)$ if and only if the remainder $r = 0$, which occurs if and only if $p(a) = 0$.

units.equation_conditions: Valid for any polynomial $p(x)$ with coefficients over a field and linear divisor $(x - a)$.
units.worked_problem_stem: Determine whether $(x + 2)$ is a factor of $p(x) = x^3 + 3x^2 + 5x + 6$.
worked_steps: Set the divisor to zero: $x + 2 = 0 \implies x = -2$.
Since $p(-2) = 0$, by the Factor Theorem $(x + 2)$ is an exact factor of $p(x)$.
units.svg_caption: Factor Theorem Logic: Divisor Setup $\to$ Root Nullification $\to$ Factorization Criterion.
units.svg_body: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 160" width="100%" height="auto"><g data-g9-stage-id="s1"><rect x="20" y="15" width="400" height="36" rx="6" fill="#eff6ff" stroke="#3b82f6"/><text x="220" y="38" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#1e40af">p(x) = (x - a)q(x) + r</text></g><g data-g9-stage-id="s2"><rect x="20" y="60" width="400" height="36" rx="6" fill="#fef3c7" stroke="#f59e0b"/><text x="220" y="83" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#92400e">x = a ⟹ p(a) = 0·q(a) + r = r</text></g><g data-g9-stage-id="s3"><rect x="20" y="105" width="400" height="40" rx="8" fill="#dcfce7" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="2"/><text x="220" y="130" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#166534">r = 0 ⟺ p(a) = 0 ⟹ (x - a) is a factor</text></g></svg>
units.trap_wrong_idea: Evaluating $p(a)$ when the divisor is $(x + a)$ instead of using the root $x = -a$.
units.trap_diagnostic: If $(x + 4)$ divides $p(x)$, what value must evaluate to zero?
units.trap_repair_explanation: Find the zero of the factor: $x + 4 = 0 \implies x = -4$. Hence $p(-4) = 0$, not $p(4) = 0$.
units.triad_check: What is the remainder when $p(x)$ is divided by $(x - c)$?
units.triad_apply: Find $k$ such that $(x - 1)$ is a factor of $x^3 - 3x^2 + kx - 4$.
units.triad_connect: How does the Factor Theorem allow decomposing degree $n$ polynomials into products of linear and irreducible quadratic factors?

exit_task.prompt: Using the Factor Theorem, prove that $(x - 2)$ is a factor of $p(x) = x^3 - 8$. Verify your result by factoring $x^3 - 8$ directly using an algebraic identity.
exit_task.answer: Evaluate $p(2) = 2^3 - 8 = 8 - 8 = 0$. Since $p(2) = 0$, by the Factor Theorem $(x - 2)$ is a factor of $x^3 - 8$.
exit_task.check: Algebraic identity check: $x^3 - 2^3 = (x - 2)(x^2 + 2x + 4)$. Divisibility is verified algebraically.
